content:
A local business in Pune should add LocalBusiness structured data to its website because it gives Google a clean, machine-readable statement of the business name, address, phone number and opening hours, and because it makes the website's version of those facts match your Google Business Profile. It will not, by itself, put you in the map pack or lift your rankings, and anyone who sells it as a ranking trick is overselling. What it does is remove ambiguity. If you are looking for a web development company in Pune that handles this properly, this guide explains what the markup contains, which properties Google actually asks for, how to write opening hours that do not break, how to handle more than one branch, and how to test the result. It is written for owners of clinics, coaching classes, salons, law and accounting practices, restaurants and shops, and for the developer or agency who will implement it.

Everything about what Google supports comes from Google Search Central's documentation on local business structured data and its general structured data guidelines. Where we describe our own practice from building and maintaining websites, we say so. We do not quote any ranking improvement or traffic figure, because Google publishes none for this markup and an invented number would be worth less than none.

## What LocalBusiness markup is, in plain terms

Structured data is a block of code on a page that describes the page's subject in a vocabulary shared by search engines, called schema.org. For a local business, the relevant type is `LocalBusiness`, or one of its more specific subtypes such as `Dentist`, `LegalService`, `Restaurant`, `HairSalon`, `AccountingService` or `Store`. Google recommends JSON-LD as the format, which means the data sits in a single script tag in the page rather than being woven into the visible HTML.

A reader never sees the JSON-LD block, and that is not a problem. Structured data is allowed to be invisible as code, but the facts inside it must be visible to a human somewhere on the same page. Google's guidelines say structured data should represent content that is actually on the page and must not mislead. So if the markup says you are open until 8 pm, the page should say so in words, and your Google Business Profile should agree. That consistency is the whole point.

## What it does and does not do

It helps to be exact about the claims, because this topic attracts exaggeration.

**What it can do.** It lets Google read your name, address, phone, hours and a few other facts directly rather than guessing them from page text. It can help Google connect the website to the right business entity, particularly when the name or address is written in several different ways across the web. It supports the information shown in some search features.

**What it does not do.** Google's documentation describes structured data as helping it understand content and making a page eligible for certain features. It does not promise a feature, and it does not promise a ranking boost. The local map results, the "map pack", are driven mainly by your Google Business Profile, together with relevance, distance and prominence signals that Google describes in its own help pages. A website's schema is a supporting signal at most. If your Business Profile is unverified, has the wrong category or has inconsistent details, no website markup will repair it. For the profile side, our guide to [getting Google reviews legitimately and keeping your profile safe](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-reviews-2026/) and our overview of [local SEO and the Google map pack in Pune](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026/) cover the other half of the job.

## The properties Google asks for

Google's local business documentation separates required and recommended properties. As we read the current guidance:

- **Required:** `name` and `address`. The address should be a `PostalAddress` with its parts filled in: street address, locality, region, postal code and country.
- **Recommended:** `telephone`, `url`, `geo` (latitude and longitude), `openingHoursSpecification`, `priceRange`, `image`, and for businesses with departments or several roles, the `department` property. A `sameAs` list pointing to your official profiles is also commonly included.

Treat the list as a minimum to meet and a checklist to extend, not a competition to fill every field. A property you cannot keep accurate is worse than one you leave out. A `priceRange` that is two years old, for example, is a quiet source of mismatch.

## A worked example

The following is an illustration created for this article. The business, address and numbers are invented and are not a client. Replace every value with your own, and do not copy the example's phone number.

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "PhysiotherapyClinic",
  "@id": "https://www.example-clinic.in/#clinic",
  "name": "Example Physio Clinic",
  "url": "https://www.example-clinic.in/",
  "image": "https://www.example-clinic.in/images/clinic-front.jpg",
  "telephone": "+91-20-0000-0000",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "12 Example Road, Kothrud",
    "addressLocality": "Pune",
    "addressRegion": "Maharashtra",
    "postalCode": "411038",
    "addressCountry": "IN"
  },
  "geo": { "@type": "GeoCoordinates", "latitude": 18.5000, "longitude": 73.8000 },
  "openingHoursSpecification": [
    {
      "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
      "dayOfWeek": ["Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday"],
      "opens": "09:00",
      "closes": "19:00"
    },
    {
      "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
      "dayOfWeek": "Saturday",
      "opens": "09:00",
      "closes": "13:00"
    }
  ],
  "sameAs": [ "https://www.facebook.com/example-clinic" ]
}
```

A few details in that block are worth explaining, because they are where real implementations go wrong.

**Use the most specific type that is honest.** `PhysiotherapyClinic` is better than `LocalBusiness` if it fits, because it tells Google more. But do not stretch. A clinic that also sells a few products is still a clinic. Schema.org lists the subtypes, and Google's documentation points to that list.

**Give the entity an `@id`.** The `@id` is a stable identifier, usually the home page URL plus a fragment. It lets you refer to the same business from other blocks, for example from an `Organization` block or from a `Service` or `Article` block, without duplicating the details.

**Write hours in 24-hour format.** `09:00` and `19:00`, not `9 AM` or `7 pm`. Days are written in English as schema.org names them, regardless of the language of your site.

**Prefer `openingHoursSpecification` for anything non-trivial.** It handles split shifts and exceptions better than the shorter `openingHours` text form. Two ranges on the same day, for example a lunch break, are written as two specifications for that day.

## Opening hours that do not break

Hours are the field that goes stale fastest, and wrong hours do real damage: someone travels across Pune to a closed door. Some practical points:

- **Closed days are simply left out.** If you are closed on Sunday, do not list Sunday. Google's documentation also describes a convention for a closed day expressed as opening and closing at the same time; leaving the day out is the simpler route and what we use.
- **A split day needs two entries.** A clinic open 10:00 to 13:00 and 17:00 to 20:00 is two specifications for each such day.
- **Holiday and festival closures** are expressed with `validFrom` and `validThrough` on a specification. This is worth the effort around Diwali, Ganeshotsav and Gudi Padwa for shops and restaurants. The rule we follow is that a temporary closure is set in the Business Profile first, because that is where most people will see it, and then mirrored on the site.
- **Open 24 hours** is written as opening at `00:00` and closing at `23:59`.
- **By appointment only** businesses should say so in visible text. Do not publish hours in markup that suggest walk-ins are welcome if they are not.

Who maintains it matters more than how it is written. If the hours live in a plugin setting, a footer widget and a markup template in three places, one will drift. Our practice is to keep the hours in a single place, such as one theme setting or one data file, and generate the footer text, the contact page and the JSON-LD from it. Then a change is made once.

## Name, address and phone: the consistency rule

Local search professionals use the shorthand "NAP" for name, address and phone. The useful rule is simple: write them the same way everywhere you control. If your Business Profile says "Shop 4, Landmark Plaza" and your site says "Landmark Plaza, Shop No. 4" the difference is probably harmless to a human, but you gain nothing from the inconsistency and you may lose a little clarity, so pick one form.

Some Pune-specific points:

- **Use the real registered trading name** that appears on your signboard and your Business Profile. Adding keywords such as "Best Dentist in Pune" to the `name` property is the sort of thing Google's guidelines for Business Profile names prohibit, and putting it in markup copies the problem onto your site.
- **Landmarks and areas.** Pune addresses lean on landmarks. Keep the street address in `streetAddress` and let the area, for example Kothrud, Baner or Parvati, go in `addressLocality` only if that is how the post office and your Business Profile write it. For the neighbourhood pages question, see our guide to [service-area pages without creating doorway pages](/blog/website-designer-pune-service-area-location-pages-doorway-2026/).
- **Phone format.** Use the international format with the country code, `+91`, in the markup. On the visible page, write it the way local customers expect to read it.

## Which page gets the markup

For a single-location business, put the `LocalBusiness` block on the home page and the contact page. Both describe the same entity, and using the same `@id` on both keeps them linked.

For a business with several branches, Google's guidance, and our own practice, is to give each branch its own page with its own markup, describing that branch only. A block on the home page that lists nine addresses is hard to interpret. A page for the Baner branch, with its own address, hours, phone and a map, is clear. Each page must hold real, specific information, such as the branch team, local directions and parking, not the same paragraph with the area name swapped. That is the line between a useful branch page and a doorway page, and the page that crosses it can hurt rather than help.

For a service business with no public premises, such as a plumber or an interior designer working from a home office, the question is what to publish. Google distinguishes businesses with a storefront from service-area businesses, and a service-area business can hide its address in the Business Profile. If you do not want your home address public, do not put it in markup either. In that case, use `areaServed` to state where you work and leave the street address off the public page. Do not invent a premises.

## Things to leave out

Some commonly seen additions are better avoided.

**Self-serving review markup.** It is tempting to add `aggregateRating` to your own `LocalBusiness` block with your Google star average. Google's review snippet guidelines say that reviews or ratings of a local business or organisation that are written or marked up by the business itself, which Google calls self-serving, are not eligible for review rich results. At best it does nothing. At worst, copying ratings you cannot verify onto the page creates a mismatch with the genuine reviews. Show real testimonials in visible text, with permission, and leave the markup out.

**Invented details.** No `priceRange` you do not stand behind, no `geo` coordinates guessed from a rough map pin, no photos you do not hold the rights to.

**Keyword stuffing in `description`.** The `description` property is not a place for a list of search phrases. If you include it, write one honest sentence.

**Markup for content that is not on the page.** If the markup lists services the page does not discuss, remove it. This is the exact pattern Google's structured data policies warn against.

## The relationship with your other structured data

A local business site usually carries more than one block. A typical, sensible set is:

- A `LocalBusiness` (or subtype) block on the home and contact pages.
- A `BreadcrumbList` on inner pages, which we describe in our guide to [internal links, breadcrumbs and site architecture](/blog/web-development-company-pune-internal-linking-breadcrumbs-site-architecture-2026/).
- An `Article` or `BlogPosting` block on blog posts.
- A `FAQPage` block only where a visible question and answer section exists on the page.

For the wider picture of what schema is available and what Google does with it, read our guide to [structured data and schema markup for a business website](/blog/web-development-company-pune-structured-data-schema-markup-2026/). Whatever you add, one rule holds: every block must be a faithful summary of the visible page.

## How to add it

How you add the markup depends on how the site is built.

**WordPress.** SEO plugins such as Yoast SEO, Rank Math and similar tools provide a local business or organisation setting that outputs the block. That is usually the fastest route. Check the output rather than assuming; plugins fill fields from settings that may be empty or outdated. If you add JSON-LD by hand through a theme file or a header-injection plugin, make sure the plugin is not also outputting its own `LocalBusiness` block, because two conflicting blocks on one page are worse than one.

**Shopify and other hosted builders.** Many themes output organisation data but not a full local business block. A hand-added JSON-LD block in the theme's template is the usual solution, with the same caution about duplicates.

**Custom-built sites.** A single reusable component fed by one data file for name, address, phone and hours is the cleanest way, and it is how we prefer to build for local clients on our [website creation service](/services/website-creation/).

**Tag Manager.** Injecting JSON-LD through Google Tag Manager works, and Google has said it can read dynamically injected markup, but it adds a dependency and a failure point. For a small site we favour having the markup in the page template instead.

## Testing and monitoring

After adding the markup, check it:

1. **Rich Results Test.** Google's tool lets you paste a URL or code and shows the detected structured data and any errors or warnings. A local business block may not show a rich result preview, because local business markup is not tied to one. The test still reports whether the block parses and whether required properties are present.
2. **Schema Markup Validator.** The schema.org validator checks the syntax against the vocabulary rather than against Google's feature rules. Use it as a second opinion.
3. **Search Console.** Once the site is verified, the enhancement and structured data reports show detected items and errors over time, and the URL Inspection tool shows what Google found on a specific page.
4. **View source.** Open the live page, view the source, and read the block. Confirm the phone number, the address and the hours match what a visitor sees.

Then put a recurring check in the calendar. We suggest a review whenever the hours, address, phone, or Business Profile change, and a routine check at least every quarter. Stale markup is the usual failure, not broken syntax.

## A short audit you can do today

If your site already has local business markup, spend fifteen minutes on this list.

1. Open your Google Business Profile and note the name, address, phone and hours.
2. Open your site's contact page and compare the visible details.
3. View the page source and find the JSON-LD block. Compare again.
4. Check that the business type is the most specific honest subtype.
5. Check that there is exactly one `LocalBusiness` block per page, not two from different plugins.
6. Check that there is no `aggregateRating` you wrote yourself.
7. Run the page through the Rich Results Test and read the warnings.
8. Check that holiday hours, if shown, are current.

## What to put in a brief or contract

If you are asking an agency or freelancer to add this, ask for the following in writing:

- Which type will be used and why.
- Where the single source of truth for name, address, phone and hours will live.
- Which pages will carry the block, and confirmation that branch pages describe only their own branch.
- A test report, with the Rich Results Test output and a source-view check, delivered at launch.
- Confirmation that no self-serving review markup and no hidden text is included.
- Who updates the data when hours change, and how.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does LocalBusiness schema help me rank in the Google map pack?

Not directly. The map results are driven mainly by your Google Business Profile, plus relevance, distance and prominence. LocalBusiness markup helps Google read and confirm the facts on your website, and it must match your profile, but Google does not promise a ranking benefit from it.

### Which properties are required for LocalBusiness structured data?

Google's documentation lists name and address as required, with a complete postal address. It recommends telephone, url, geo, opening hours, price range and image, among others. Fill in only what you can keep accurate.

### Should I add star ratings to my LocalBusiness markup?

No. Google says reviews or ratings that a business writes or marks up about itself, called self-serving, are not eligible for review rich results. Show genuine testimonials as visible text instead.

### How do I mark up more than one branch?

Give each branch its own page with its own markup, describing only that branch, with real local details such as address, hours, team and directions. A single block listing every branch on the home page is harder for search engines to interpret.

### Can I use JSON-LD if my site is on WordPress or Shopify?

Yes. WordPress SEO plugins can output it from settings, and Shopify themes can carry a hand-added block. Check the live output, and make sure two plugins or the theme and a plugin are not each outputting a conflicting block.
